entries.lesson_core_move: Identify whether a continuous-time signal is periodic or aperiodic by testing for a finite repeating period and linking aperiodicity to the need for Fourier-transform analysis.

sections.section_title: Testing a Signal for a Finite Repeating Period

prompt_blocks.text: Determine whether $x(t)=\cos(4t)+\cos(6t)$ is periodic, and if it is, choose a valid repeat period.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The component periods are $\pi/2$ for $\cos(4t)$ and $\pi/3$ for $\cos(6t)$. The signal repeats after a finite common period, and $\pi$ works because it is a multiple of both component periods.

prompt_blocks.text: Determine whether $x(t)=\sin(3t)+\cos(5t)$ is periodic, and if it is, choose the smallest valid repeat period.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The component periods are $2\pi/3$ and $2\pi/5$. The smallest finite period that works for both terms is $2\pi$, so the signal is periodic.

sections.section_title: Identifying Aperiodic Signals from Failed Period Tests

prompt_blocks.text: Is $x(t)=\cos(2t)+\cos(\sqrt{2}t)$ periodic or aperiodic?

choice_blocks.text: Cannot determine from the form alone

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The two terms repeat on their own, but the whole signal would need one finite common repeat time. Their periods are $\pi$ and $\sqrt{2}\pi$, and those are not commensurate, so no finite $T>0$ works. The signal is aperiodic.

prompt_blocks.text: Is $x(t)=\cos(t)+\cos(\sqrt{5}t)$ periodic or aperiodic?

choice_blocks.text: Cannot determine from the form alone

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The component periods are $2\pi$ and $2\pi/\sqrt{5}$. Since those periods are not commensurate, there is no finite $T>0$ that repeats both terms, so the signal is aperiodic.

sections.section_title: Choosing Fourier Series or Fourier Transform Analysis from Periodicity

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=\cos(2t)+\sin(2t)$, which analysis framework is appropriate?

choice_blocks.text: Both Fourier series and Fourier transform
Neither Fourier series nor Fourier transform

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal is periodic because both terms have the same angular frequency $2$, so it repeats with a finite period. Periodic signals are analyzed with Fourier series, so choice A is correct.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=\cos(t)+\cos(\sqrt{5}t)$, which analysis framework is appropriate?

choice_blocks.text: Both Fourier series and Fourier transform
Neither Fourier series nor Fourier transform

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The angular frequencies $1$ and $\sqrt{5}$ have an irrational ratio, so the sum has no finite repeating period. Aperiodic signals are analyzed with Fourier transform, so choice B is correct.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret an aperiodic signal as the infinite-period limit of a periodic extension to connect Fourier-series harmonics with the Fourier-transform viewpoint.

sections.section_title: Building a Periodic Extension from One Signal Copy

prompt_blocks.text: A signal copy $z(t)$ is nonzero on $0 \le t < 2$. Which option correctly describes a periodic extension with period $T=6$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Choice B is correct because it repeats the same unchanged copy every $6$ units. Choice A uses the wrong spacing, C stretches the copy instead of translating it, D changes the amplitude, and E keeps only one copy instead of repeating it periodically.

prompt_blocks.text: A signal copy $w(t)$ is nonzero on $-1 \le t < 1$. Which option correctly describes a periodic extension with period $T=5$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Choice B is correct because it repeats the same copy every $5$ units without changing its shape. A uses the wrong repeat spacing, C compresses the copy, D changes the amplitude, and E keeps just one copy instead of extending it periodically.

sections.section_title: Increasing the Period While Preserving the Signal Copy

prompt_blocks.text: Two periodic extensions use the same signal copy, one with period $T_1=6$ and one with period $T_2=18$. Which statement is correct?

choice_blocks.text: The same copy is repeated farther apart.
The same copy is stretched to fill each longer period.
The copies are closer together when the period is larger.
The waveform amplitude changes when the period changes.
The two extensions have identical spacing because they use the same copy.

questions.correct_answer: The same copy is repeated farther apart.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The copy itself is preserved, so the only change from $T_1=6$ to $T_2=18$ is the spacing between repeats. A larger period means wider gaps, not a stretched or reshaped copy.
So the correct statement is that the same copy is repeated farther apart.

prompt_blocks.text: If the period increases from $T=8$ to $T=24$ while the signal copy is preserved, which feature stays fixed?

choice_blocks.text: The waveform copy itself stays the same.
The waveform copy gets compressed into a shorter shape.
The repeated copies move closer together.
The waveform amplitude increases with the period.
The spacing between copies stays fixed even though the period changes.

questions.correct_answer: The waveform copy itself stays the same.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Increasing the period does not reshape the waveform copy. It only moves the repeated copies farther apart, so the copy itself stays fixed.
So the fixed feature is the waveform copy itself.

sections.section_title: Taking the Infinite-Period Limit of the Extension

prompt_blocks.text: As the period of the periodic extension grows from $T=6$ toward infinity, what happens on any fixed finite time window?

choice_blocks.text: The waveform is stretched horizontally, but the repeats stay the same distance apart.
The repeated copies move farther apart, so the window approaches the original aperiodic signal.
The signal becomes identically zero outside the window.
Only the amplitudes of the copies change while the spacing stays finite.
The signal remains exactly periodic with period $6$.

questions.correct_answer: The repeated copies move farther apart, so the window approaches the original aperiodic signal.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The copy of $x(t)$ is unchanged; only the spacing between repeats increases. On a fixed finite window, the extra copies move out of view, so the local signal approaches the original aperiodic signal.

prompt_blocks.text: Which statement best describes the limit $\lim_{T\to\infty} x_T(t)$ on a fixed finite window?

choice_blocks.text: It says the signal stays globally periodic, but with a larger and larger finite period.
It says the copy itself is stretched while the repeat spacing stays fixed.
It says the local window converges to $x(t)$ even though each finite-$T$ signal is periodic.
It says the signal becomes zero everywhere except at the origin.
It says only the amplitudes of the repeated copies change.

questions.correct_answer: It says the local window converges to $x(t)$ even though each finite-$T$ signal is periodic.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The limit is local in time. As $T$ grows, the repeats move apart, but the waveform copy stays the same, so the fixed window converges to the original aperiodic signal.

sections.section_title: Connecting the Infinite-Period Limit to the Fourier Transform Viewpoint

prompt_blocks.text: As $T\to\infty$, what happens to the Fourier-series harmonics of the periodic extension $x_T(t)$?

choice_blocks.text: The harmonic spacing shrinks, so the discrete lines crowd together and the frequency picture becomes continuous.
The harmonic spacing grows, so the discrete lines spread farther apart and remain isolated.
The harmonics disappear because the signal becomes aperiodic.
Only the time-domain waveform changes; the frequency interpretation stays a fixed discrete set of lines.
The Fourier transform applies only to periodic signals, so the periodic-extension view must be kept.

questions.correct_answer: The harmonic spacing shrinks, so the discrete lines crowd together and the frequency picture becomes continuous.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Increasing $T$ makes the fundamental spacing smaller, so the harmonic grid gets denser. That discrete-to-continuous transition is exactly why the Fourier-transform viewpoint becomes natural.

prompt_blocks.text: Which statement best explains why the original aperiodic signal is naturally analyzed with the Fourier transform viewpoint as the period grows without bound?

choice_blocks.text: As $\omega_0\to 0$, the harmonic grid becomes denser, so the discrete Fourier-series picture approaches a continuous-frequency description.
As $\omega_0\to 0$, the harmonic grid becomes sparser, so the spectrum stays a set of isolated lines.
As $T$ grows, the signal becomes periodic enough that Fourier series replaces Fourier transform.
The time-domain copy changes, but the frequency grid does not change at all.
The Fourier transform is only for periodic signals, so the periodic extension remains the final analysis form.

questions.correct_answer: As $\omega_0\to 0$, the harmonic grid becomes denser, so the discrete Fourier-series picture approaches a continuous-frequency description.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The point of the limit is not that the signal stops having structure. The point is that the discrete harmonics of the periodic extension crowd together until the frequency description is naturally read on a continuous axis, which is the Fourier-transform viewpoint.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the Fourier-series frequency spacing omega_0 = 2*pi/T and interpret how it shrinks toward continuous frequency as the period grows without bound.

sections.section_title: Computing Frequency Spacing from the Period

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal has period $T=2$ s. What is its Fourier-series spacing $\omega_0$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $\omega_0=2\pi/T$ and substitute $T=2$ s.
So the Fourier-series spacing is $\pi\text{ rad/s}$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal has period $T=250$ ms. What is its Fourier-series spacing $\omega_0$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Convert $250$ ms to $0.25$ s, then use $\omega_0=2\pi/T$.
So the Fourier-series spacing is $8\pi\text{ rad/s}$.

sections.section_title: Finding Harmonic Frequencies from the Spacing

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal has period $T=4$ s. Which choice gives the first three positive harmonic frequencies?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T$. With $T=4$ s, $\omega_0 = \pi/2$, and then $\omega_n = n\omega_0$ gives $\omega_1 = \pi/2$, $\omega_2 = \pi$, and $\omega_3 = 3\pi/2$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal has period $T=0.5$ s. Which choice gives the first three positive harmonic frequencies?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T$. With $T=0.5$ s, $\omega_0 = 4\pi$, and then $\omega_n = n\omega_0$ gives $\omega_1 = 4\pi$, $\omega_2 = 8\pi$, and $\omega_3 = 12\pi$.

sections.section_title: Comparing Frequency Spacing for Larger Periods

prompt_blocks.text: If one signal has period $T$ and another has period $4T$, which statement about the Fourier-series spacing is correct?

choice_blocks.text: The $4T$ signal has spacing $4\omega_0$, so its harmonic lines are farther apart.
The $4T$ signal has spacing $\omega_0$, so the spacing is unchanged.
The $4T$ signal has spacing $\omega_0/4$, so its harmonic spectrum is denser.
The $T$ signal has spacing $\omega_0/4$, so its harmonic spectrum is denser.
The $4T$ signal has spacing $\omega_0/4$, but its harmonic spectrum is sparser.

questions.correct_answer: The $4T$ signal has spacing $\omega_0/4$, so its harmonic spectrum is denser.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T$. Replacing $T$ by $4T$ makes the spacing one-fourth as large, so the harmonic lines move closer together.
So the larger-period signal has the denser harmonic spectrum.

prompt_blocks.text: Between a signal with period $T$ and a signal with period $5T$, which harmonic spectrum is denser?

choice_blocks.text: The $T$ spectrum is denser because its spacing is larger.
The $T$ spectrum is denser because the period is smaller.
The $5T$ spectrum is denser because its spacing is $\omega_0/5$.
The $5T$ spectrum is denser because its spacing is $5\omega_0$.
Both spectra have the same density because only the harmonic index changes.

questions.correct_answer: The $5T$ spectrum is denser because its spacing is $\omega_0/5$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The spacing rule is inverse in the period: $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T$. If the period grows to $5T$, the spacing shrinks to one-fifth of the original.
So the larger-period signal is the one with the denser harmonic spectrum.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Frequency Spacing as the Period Grows Without Bound

prompt_blocks.text: As $T\to\infty$, what happens to $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Since $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T$, the denominator grows without bound as $T\to\infty$, so the spacing shrinks to $0$.

prompt_blocks.text: When $T$ grows without bound and $\omega_0$ collapses to zero, what is the best interpretation of the Fourier-series harmonic lines?

choice_blocks.text: They crowd together and approach a continuous frequency axis.
They spread farther apart because the period is increasing.
The spectrum changes from frequency to time.

questions.correct_answer: They crowd together and approach a continuous frequency axis.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: When the spacing tends to $0$, the harmonic lines become arbitrarily dense, which is the bridge from discrete Fourier-series lines to a continuous frequency axis.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret continuous frequency as the variable that replaces discrete harmonic indices when the Fourier-series period grows without bound.

sections.section_title: Identifying Discrete Harmonic Frequencies

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal has period $T = 6$ s. Which set lists the harmonic frequencies for $n = -2,-1,0,1,2$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The period tells us to use the Fourier-series harmonic grid, where $\omega_n = n\omega_0$.
Multiply $\omega_0$ by each integer index. The harmonic frequencies are $-\frac{2\pi}{3}$, $-\frac{\pi}{3}$, $0$, $\frac{\pi}{3}$, and $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ rad/s.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal has period $T = 8$ s. Which set lists the harmonic frequencies for $n = -3,-2,-1,0,1$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same harmonic-grid rule: $\omega_n = n\omega_0$.
Multiply $\omega_0$ by the integer indices. The harmonic frequencies are $-\frac{3\pi}{4}$, $-\frac{\pi}{2}$, $-\frac{\pi}{4}$, $0$, and $\frac{\pi}{4}$ rad/s.

sections.section_title: Seeing Frequency Samples Become Denser

prompt_blocks.text: Compare periodic signals with periods $T = 3$ s and $T = 12$ s. Which statement is correct about the harmonic grid?

choice_blocks.text: The $T = 12$ s signal has the denser harmonic grid because its harmonic spacing is smaller.
The $T = 3$ s signal has the denser harmonic grid because its harmonic spacing is smaller.
Both signals have the same harmonic spacing because the period does not affect $\omega_0$.
The $T = 3$ s signal has the denser harmonic grid because it has more harmonic coefficients.
The $T = 12$ s signal has the denser harmonic grid because increasing $T$ makes the spacing larger.

questions.correct_answer: The $T = 12$ s signal has the denser harmonic grid because its harmonic spacing is smaller.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $\omega_0 = \frac{2\pi}{T}$. A larger period gives a smaller harmonic spacing, so the $T = 12$ s grid is denser than the $T = 3$ s grid.

prompt_blocks.text: Using ordinary frequency $f_0 = 1/T$, compare signals with periods $T = 5$ s and $T = 20$ s. Which statement is correct about the harmonic grid?

choice_blocks.text: The $T = 20$ s signal has the denser harmonic grid because its spacing in $f$ is smaller.
The $T = 5$ s signal has the denser harmonic grid because its spacing in $f$ is smaller.
Both signals have the same density because changing from $\omega$ to $f$ does not change spacing.
The $T = 5$ s signal has the denser harmonic grid because it has more harmonic coefficients.
The $T = 20$ s signal has the denser harmonic grid because increasing $T$ makes the spacing in $f$ larger.

questions.correct_answer: The $T = 20$ s signal has the denser harmonic grid because its spacing in $f$ is smaller.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $f_0 = 1/T$. The larger period has the smaller spacing in ordinary frequency, so the $T = 20$ s grid is denser.

sections.section_title: Replacing Harmonic Indices with a Frequency Variable

prompt_blocks.text: When the period becomes arbitrarily large, which symbol replaces the discrete harmonic index on the spectrum?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: As $T \to \infty$, the spacing $\omega_0 = \frac{2\pi}{T}$ collapses to $0$, so the harmonic grid stops being indexed by integers. The spectrum is then labeled by the continuous frequency variable $\omega$.

prompt_blocks.text: As the harmonic spacing collapses, what symbol should replace $n$ in the notation $f_n = \frac{n}{T}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The same limit replaces the discrete harmonic index with a frequency variable. In this notation, that continuous variable is $f$, not the period, spacing, index, or coefficient.

sections.section_title: Reading a Spectrum on a Continuous Frequency Axis

prompt_blocks.text: A spectrum is written as $X(\omega)$ on a continuous frequency axis, and you want the value at $\omega = 0.75\pi$ rad/s. Which interpretation is correct?

choice_blocks.text: The value is invalid because only integer harmonic labels are allowed.
Read $\omega$ as the axis coordinate and take the spectrum value at that frequency.
Treat $0.75\pi$ as the harmonic index $n$ and multiply by $\omega_0$.
Interpret the request as a time-domain value at $t = 0.75\pi$.
The spectrum has no meaningful label at noninteger frequencies.

questions.correct_answer: Read $\omega$ as the axis coordinate and take the spectrum value at that frequency.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: On a continuous frequency axis, $\omega$ is the coordinate itself, so $0.75\pi$ rad/s names a valid location. You read $X(\omega)$ at that point rather than forcing it onto an integer harmonic grid.

prompt_blocks.text: A spectrum is written as $X(j\omega)$ on a continuous frequency axis, and you want the value at $\omega = -1.2\pi$ rad/s. Which interpretation is correct?

choice_blocks.text: It is a coordinate only when $\omega$ is an integer multiple of $\omega_0$.
It is the time variable of the signal.
It is a coordinate on the continuous axis, so the spectrum can be read there directly.
It must be converted to a harmonic index before reading.
It has no meaning unless the signal is periodic.

questions.correct_answer: It is a coordinate on the continuous axis, so the spectrum can be read there directly.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: In the continuous-frequency setting, $\omega$ labels a point on the axis, so $-1.2\pi$ rad/s is just another valid location. It is not restricted to integer harmonic locations the way a Fourier-series grid is.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the Fourier transform definition to convert an aperiodic continuous-time signal x(t) into its continuous-frequency spectrum X(j omega).

sections.section_title: Substituting a Signal into the Fourier Transform Integral

prompt_blocks.text: Which option correctly substitutes $x(t)=2$ for $-T/4 \le t \le T/4$ and $0$ otherwise into the Fourier transform definition for $X(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The Fourier-transform definition keeps the limits at $-\infty$ to $\infty$ and inserts the given $x(t)$ directly into the integrand.
Option C matches that structure. The other choices either change the sign, switch to a Fourier-series sum, truncate the limits too early, or use the wrong amplitude.

prompt_blocks.text: Which option correctly substitutes $x(t)=1$ for $0 \le t \le T$ and $0$ otherwise into the Fourier transform definition for $X(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The correct substitution keeps the Fourier-transform kernel $e^{-j\omega t}$ and replaces $x(t)$ with its piecewise definition inside the infinite-time integral.
Option A is correct. The other choices either shorten the limits too early, switch to a Fourier-series sum, reverse the piecewise regions, or change the sign or support.

sections.section_title: Setting Integration Limits from Aperiodic Signal Support

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=0$ outside $-T \le t \le T$, which option gives the correct integration bounds for $X(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support is exactly $-T \le t \le T$, so the Fourier transform integral keeps only those bounds. The infinite interval is too wide, and the other intervals do not match the nonzero support.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=0$ outside $0 \le t \le T$, which option gives the correct integration bounds for $X(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal is nonzero only on $0 \le t \le T$, so the transform limits must match that interval exactly. Symmetric, reversed, or infinite bounds do not respect the support.

sections.section_title: Evaluating X(j omega) as a Function of Continuous Frequency

prompt_blocks.text: Which option is the correct closed-form evaluation of $X(j\omega)=\int_{-T/2}^{T/2} 2e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The constant factor $2$ doubles the pulse transform. Since $\int_{-T/2}^{T/2} e^{-j\omega t}\,dt=\frac{2\sin(\omega T/2)}{\omega}$, the result is $\frac{4\sin(\omega T/2)}{\omega}$. The removable value at $\omega=0$ is $2T$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which option is the correct closed-form evaluation of $X(j\omega)=\int_{-T}^{T} 3e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support is now $[-T,T]$, so the same antiderivative-and-boundary evaluation gives $3\cdot \frac{2\sin(\omega T)}{\omega}=\frac{6\sin(\omega T)}{\omega}$. The removable value at $\omega=0$ is $6T$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Transform Result as a Continuous-Frequency Spectrum

prompt_blocks.text: Which option correctly interprets the resulting $X(j\omega)=\frac{2\sin(\omega T/2)}{\omega}$ as a continuous-frequency spectrum?

choice_blocks.text: It assigns a value to every real $\omega$, so the transform is a continuous-frequency spectrum.
It is a discrete Fourier-series coefficient list indexed by integers.
It is only the value at $\omega=0$.
It is defined only at integer frequency indices.
It is one frequency sample that cannot be evaluated for other $\omega$.

questions.correct_answer: It assigns a value to every real $\omega$, so the transform is a continuous-frequency spectrum.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the closed-form $X(j\omega)$ as a function of $\omega$. Because $\omega$ is continuous, every real frequency gets a value. That makes the result a continuous-frequency spectrum, not a discrete harmonic list or a single sample.
The value at $\omega=0$ is just one point on that spectrum.

prompt_blocks.text: What does the value $X(0)=T$ tell you about this transform?

choice_blocks.text: The zero-frequency component equals the pulse area, so the signal has DC content of size $T$.
The spectrum is defined only at $\omega=0$.
The transform is a discrete list of harmonics spaced by integer indices.
The pulse has no low-frequency content because its transform is continuous.
The value $T$ is the time-domain amplitude of $x(t)$ for all $t$.

questions.correct_answer: The zero-frequency component equals the pulse area, so the signal has DC content of size $T$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: At $\omega=0$, the transform reports the DC component. Here that value is $T$, which matches the area of the finite pulse.
So the correct interpretation is that the pulse contributes $T$ units of zero-frequency content, not that the spectrum is discrete or defined only at one point.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the inverse Fourier transform to reconstruct an aperiodic continuous-time signal x(t) from its continuous-frequency spectrum X(j omega).

sections.section_title: Writing the Inverse Fourier Transform Integral

prompt_blocks.text: Given the continuous-frequency spectrum $X(j\omega)$, which option shows the correct inverse-transform setup for $x(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The inverse Fourier transform uses the spectrum as the integrand, the $\frac{1}{2\pi}$ scale factor, and the reconstruction kernel $e^{j\omega t}$ over all frequencies. Choice A matches that setup exactly; the other options switch direction, drop the normalization, flip the sign, or use the wrong variable inside the integral.

prompt_blocks.text: Given the continuous-frequency spectrum $Y(j\omega)$, which option shows the correct inverse-transform setup for $y(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The inverse-transform rule does not change when the letters change. For $Y(j\omega)$ and $y(t)$, the correct setup still uses all frequencies, the $\frac{1}{2\pi}$ factor, and the kernel $e^{j\omega t}$, so Choice C is the match.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Inverse Transform Integral

prompt_blocks.text: Evaluate the inverse Fourier transform of the even rectangular spectrum $X(j\omega)=1$ for $|\omega|\le 2\Omega$ and $0$ otherwise.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The spectrum is even and centered at zero, so the inverse integral runs over $[-2\Omega,2\Omega]$ and can be rewritten as a cosine integral before you simplify anything.
That gives $x(t)=\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\sin(2\Omega t)}{t}$, which is real and even. The only changes from the base example are the wider band and the same inverse normalization.

prompt_blocks.text: Evaluate the inverse Fourier transform of the even rectangular spectrum $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2}$ for $|\omega|\le \Omega$ and $0$ otherwise.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The spectrum is still even, but its height is $\frac{1}{2}$, so the inverse-transform result is just the base sinc scaled by that factor.
That gives $x(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{\sin(\Omega t)}{t}$. The answer stays real and even; only the amplitude scale changes.

sections.section_title: Reconstructing a Signal from a Piecewise Spectrum

prompt_blocks.text: Which time-domain expression reconstructs $x(t)$ from $X(j\omega)=2$ for $\Omega_1\le |\omega|\le \Omega_2$ and $0$ otherwise?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The spectrum is the same even band-gap shape as the worked example, just scaled by a factor of $2$. Split it into the outer rectangle minus the inner rectangle, apply the inverse transform to each piece, and then multiply the result by $2$.
Choice $A$ keeps only the outer band. Choice $C$ drops the scale factor. Choice $D$ flips the sign of the subtraction. Choice $E$ treats the gap as if the whole support were one contiguous rectangle.

prompt_blocks.text: Which time-domain expression reconstructs $x(t)$ from $X(j\omega)=1$ for $\Omega_1\le |\omega|\le \Omega_2$, $X(j\omega)=2$ for $\Omega_3\le |\omega|\le \Omega_4$, and $0$ otherwise?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Split the spectrum into two even rectangular bands. The first band contributes $\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\sin(\Omega_2 t)-\sin(\Omega_1 t)}{t}$, and the second band contributes $\frac{2}{\pi}\frac{\sin(\Omega_4 t)-\sin(\Omega_3 t)}{t}$.

Choice $A$ keeps only the outer edge of each band. Choice $B$ flips the subtraction order. Choice $D$ swaps the bands. Choice $E$ drops the linearity step and treats the whole support as one rectangle.

sections.section_title: Checking Reconstruction with the Forward Transform

prompt_blocks.text: Which forward-transform result confirms that this reconstructed signal matches the target spectrum?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use linearity and the standard pair $\frac{\sin(\Omega t)}{\pi t}\leftrightarrow 1$ on $|\omega|\le\Omega$. The $\Omega=4$ term gives the outer rectangle, and subtracting the $\Omega=1$ term removes the inner band.
That leaves a rectangle of height $1$ on $1\le|\omega|\le 4$ and $0$ elsewhere, so choice C is the only match.

prompt_blocks.text: Which forward-transform result confirms that this reconstructed signal matches the target spectrum?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor $2$ only changes the rectangle height. Apply the same forward-transform pair to each sinc term and subtract the inner band from the outer band by linearity.
That leaves a rectangle of height $2$ on $2\le|\omega|\le 5$ and $0$ elsewhere, so choice B is correct.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret Fourier transform pair notation by matching x(t) and X(j omega) to the forward and inverse transforms that connect a time-domain signal with its spectrum.

sections.section_title: Matching x(t) with X(j omega)

prompt_blocks.text: Which statement correctly matches the pair $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$?

choice_blocks.text: $x(t)$ is the time-domain signal, $X(j\omega)$ is the frequency-domain spectrum, and the pair names the forward and inverse Fourier transforms between them.
$x(t)$ is the frequency-domain spectrum, $X(j\omega)$ is the time-domain signal, and the pair names the forward and inverse Fourier transforms between them.
Both $x(t)$ and $X(j\omega)$ are time-domain signals, so the pair only rewrites one signal in a different form.
$X(j\omega)$ is the Fourier transform operator, while $x(t)$ is the transformed output.
The pair shows two unrelated labels that do not describe a transform relationship.

questions.correct_answer: $x(t)$ is the time-domain signal, $X(j\omega)$ is the frequency-domain spectrum, and the pair names the forward and inverse Fourier transforms between them.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The left symbol, $x(t)$, is the time-domain signal because the argument $t$ labels time. The right symbol, $X(j\omega)$, is the frequency-domain spectrum because the argument $j\omega$ labels continuous angular frequency.
The pair names the forward Fourier transform from $x(t)$ to $X(j\omega)$ and the inverse Fourier transform from $X(j\omega)$ back to $x(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: If a note says the pair $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ is read left to right, what transform direction does that name?

choice_blocks.text: The forward Fourier transform from $x(t)$ to $X(j\omega)$.
The inverse Fourier transform from $X(j\omega)$ to $x(t)$.
No transform direction; the pair only labels the same signal in two ways.
A transform from frequency to time that keeps the symbols in the same order.
The transform operator $\mathcal{F}$ itself, not the signal pair.

questions.correct_answer: The forward Fourier transform from $x(t)$ to $X(j\omega)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reading the pair left to right starts from the time-domain signal $x(t)$ and gives the frequency-domain spectrum $X(j\omega)$. That is the forward Fourier transform.
Reading right to left would name the inverse transform from $X(j\omega)$ back to $x(t)$.

sections.section_title: Reading the Forward Transform Direction

prompt_blocks.text: The pair notation $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ is shown. If you start from $x(t)$, which symbol is produced by the forward transform, and what domain is it in?

choice_blocks.text: $X(j\omega)$, the input signal in the time domain

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The forward transform reads from the time signal to the spectrum. Starting from $x(t)$, the output is $X(j\omega)$, and because the argument is $j\omega$, that output is in the frequency domain.

prompt_blocks.text: A reference card says the forward transform goes from $x(t)$ to the spectrum. In the pair $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is the output symbol and what domain does it represent?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Reading the notation in the forward direction means the signal $x(t)$ becomes the spectrum $X(j\omega)$. The $j\omega$ argument marks the frequency domain, so the output is $X(j\omega)$ in frequency space.

sections.section_title: Reading the Inverse Transform Direction

prompt_blocks.text: The pair notation $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ is shown. If you start from $X(j\omega)$, what do you recover with the inverse transform?

choice_blocks.text: No signal is recovered with the inverse transform.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the input symbol $X(j\omega)$. That tells you to read the pair in the spectrum-to-signal direction.
So the inverse transform recovers $x(t)$, which is the time-domain signal.

prompt_blocks.text: Which option correctly completes $X(j\omega) \xrightarrow{\mathcal{F}^{-1}} ?$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The arrow already shows the inverse direction, so the output must be the original time-domain signal.
